arguments.name: Three-proposition fake-door pre-order test with barrier survey
arguments.method: Three landing pages, equal paid ad spend to each audience: (A) fidelity music protector for musicians/concert-goers, (B) children's event/chore protection for parents with safety-brand framing, (C) Bluetooth work/yard muffs for DIYers. Each page has two price points. Visitors clicking 'reserve' leave email or refundable deposit, then a 5-question survey on main reason/barrier (sound quality vs lack of concern; child-safety trust; audio features vs brand vs price).
arguments.sample: About 1,500 visitors per proposition (about 4,500 total) in 2 European markets; survey all reservers plus a sample of non-reservers
arguments.measure: Visitor-to-reservation conversion per proposition and price; share citing each theory's causal reason; cost per reservation

prediction_by_theory.T1: A converts best in its audience even at the higher price; most non-users cite sound degradation rather than lack of concern
prediction_by_theory.T2: B converts best and is least price-sensitive; respondents cite brand safety trust
prediction_by_theory.T3: C gets clicks but conversion drops sharply at the higher price; respondents rank audio features and price above brand

arguments.decision_rule: Advance a proposition only if reservation conversion is at least 3% of visitors at the higher price AND at least 50% of its respondents cite the theory's causal reason. If C passes on conversion but over 60% rank price/features above brand, treat as commodity and do not invest. If none reaches 3%, no consumer expansion beyond existing retail.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to building a consumer proposition yet. Hellberg already reaches individual buyers through retail stores and online shops and already sells a children's product for concerts and lawn mowing. The music-fidelity use case (T1) has the best independent support for a real behavioural barrier, but specialist fidelity earplugs already exist, so Hellberg's differentiation is unproven. Run the 18,000 EUR, 10-week fake-door test X1 and invest only if a proposition passes its threshold.

result.title: Simulated wear test on comfort
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. In this simulated wear test, people given a softer, better-fitting protector wore it no more often than people given the standard one.
result.access_limitation: Synthetic. It says nothing about real demand.

arguments.reason: SYN-B is simulated and tests comfort/fit, not sound fidelity, so it cannot confirm or refute T1's mechanism; at most it is a reminder that a physical redesign need not raise wearing if the real barrier is lack of concern, which Couth et al. also name. I give it no evidential weight. The real revision comes from Minuendo and Eargasm: fidelity-preserving earplugs already exist from specialists, so even if the fidelity barrier is real, Hellberg would need a further advantage to capture value.
arguments.new_claim: Musicians and concert-goers under-use hearing protection partly because devices degrade how music sounds (with lack of concern as a rival barrier). Fidelity-preserving plugs already exist from specialists, so a new entrant captures value only if it adds something buyers value beyond fidelity, such as safety-brand trust, distribution reach or price, which remains unproven.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in building a new consumer proposition yet. Hellberg already reaches individual buyers: its own site says its products are available in many stores and online shops, and it sells Junior, a children's protector it describes for concerts, lawn mowing and sporting events. The most plausible new use case is music (musicians and concert-goers), because an independent study names sound degradation as a barrier to wearing protection. But specialist high-fidelity earplugs (Minuendo, Eargasm) already exist, so Hellberg's ability to differentiate and capture value is unproven. Run a cheap demand test before any product or channel investment, and keep no expansion as the default if the test fails.
arguments.target_customer: Provisional: early-career musicians and frequent concert-goers, tested side by side with parents buying for children and DIYers buying Bluetooth muffs
arguments.value_proposition: Hypothesis only: hearing protection that keeps music sounding clear, backed by a professional safety brand's credibility. Whether brand trust adds anything over existing specialist fidelity plugs is the open question.
arguments.next_action: Run test X1: a three-proposition fake-door pre-order test (music fidelity, children's protection, Bluetooth DIY muffs), each at two price points with a short survey on reasons and barriers, about 1,500 visitors per proposition in 2 European markets, analyst-assumed cost 18,000 EUR over 10 weeks. Advance a proposition only if reservation conversion is at least 3% at the higher price and at least 50% of respondents cite that theory's causal reason. If none passes, keep the current offering without expansion.
arguments.uncertainty: Confidence is low. I found no public sales, revenue or channel-mix data for Hellberg, so I do not know how much of its business already comes from individual buyers or from Junior. The musician study is an abstract only, does not rank the barriers, and also names lack of concern, which no product redesign can fix. The competitor pages are sellers' own claims with no sales figures. The 3M evidence shows a large incumbent already sells connected muffs through home centres and mass retail, which makes a DIY push look like a feature-and-price fight. The earplug RCT shows protection reduces temporary threshold shift, but it says nothing about willingness to buy.
would_change_if: Test X1 shows a proposition at or above 3% conversion at the higher price with a majority citing its causal reason
Evidence that lack of concern, not sound quality, is the dominant barrier for musicians (this would weaken T1 and favour no expansion)
Hellberg sales data showing Junior or retail consumer sales are already material (this would favour T2 and scaling the existing children's range instead of new development)
Evidence that buyers of connected muffs choose on safety-brand trust rather than features and price (this would rescue T3)
Evidence that specialist fidelity-earplug makers have low or stagnant sales (this would suggest the category is small)

X1.name: Three-audience fake-door landing-page test with message split
X1.method: Paid social/search ads in two European markets to three audiences: hunters/shooters, parents of children 3-12, DIY/garden prosumers. In each, randomise a use-case message (activity-tuned electronic; junior for events; consumer-styled garden) vs a control for the existing professional product. Landing page shows price and offers refundable reservation/notify-me, plus a 2-question survey: main reason for not using protection, where they first met the brand.
X1.sample: At least 400 landing-page visitors per cell (6 cells, ~2,400 visitors) over 6 weeks, plus ~15 follow-up interviews per audience
X1.measure: Reservation conversion rate per cell; cost per reservation; stated price acceptance; share citing 'cannot hear surroundings', 'child won't wear it', or 'already use at work'

prediction_by_theory.T1: Hunter/shooter use-case cell converts clearly above its professional-control cell; 'cannot hear surroundings' is a leading non-use reason
prediction_by_theory.T2: Parent use-case cell has the lowest cost per reservation of all cells; child discomfort/refusal is a leading reason
prediction_by_theory.T3: In the prosumer audience the professional-control message converts as well or better than the consumer message; most respondents first met the brand at work

X1.decision_rule: Build a differentiated proposition only for an audience whose use-case cell beats its control by >=30% relative conversion (p<0.1) AND whose cost per reservation is <=1.5x the best cell. If none qualifies and control messages are within 10% of use-case messages, accept T3: no separate consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: SYN-C is simulated and is not real evidence of demand, so it cannot overturn T3. However, it points in the same direction as the real RNID finding that a quarter of Gen Z adults would feel embarrassed to be seen wearing earplugs: appearance may drive usage, which would contradict T3's assumption that buyers value professional positioning over consumer-specific design. I keep T3 as the default, with low confidence, and flag appearance/styling as the hypothesis X1 should test (add a styled-design cell if budget allows).

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public sources show Hellberg already reaches individual buyers: a children's protector marketed for concerts, lawn mowing and sporting events, FM-radio, active-listening and Bluetooth models, and availability in 'many stores and online shops around the world'. The case for a new use-case proposition rests on unverified assumptions. Run a low-cost demand test (X1) first, and invest only in an audience that clears a pre-set threshold.
final.target_customer: Undetermined. Candidates are hunters/sport shooters (T1), parents buying for children (T2), and DIY/garden prosumers already served by the existing range (T3, the default). Young concertgoers are a possible fourth group, suggested by the RNID survey, but I did not formalise or test this as a theory.
final.value_proposition: Provisional, under T3: professional-grade protection from a brand trusted at work, sold through existing retail. A use-case variant, such as an activity-tuned electronic protector or a junior event protector, is justified only if test evidence shows it beats this.
final.next_action: Run test X1, an 8-week, roughly 16,000 EUR fake-door landing-page test across three audiences, each split between a use-case message and the professional-product message, with refundable reservations and a short survey. Build only for an audience whose use-case cell beats its control by at least 30% relative conversion (p<0.1), with cost per reservation no more than 1.5x the best cell. Consider adding a cell for styled or discreet design.
final.uncertainty: High. The evidence is mostly company self-description, which shows capability, not demand. I found no individual-vs-professional sales split, financials or retailer mix. Radians already targets hunters, which weakens T1 but does not prove saturation. RNID's non-peer-reviewed survey, with unavailable methods, hints that embarrassment about appearance limits leisure use. That would cut against T3, and no theory names it. My challenge search found nothing contradicting T3.
would_change_if: Any audience's use-case message beats the professional-control message by at least 30% at acceptable cost in X1. That would favour T1 or T2 and justify a differentiated line.
Real data show appearance or discreet design substantially raises use or purchase intent among leisure users. That would point to a styling-led proposition and against T3.
Sales or retailer data show individual buyers rarely encounter Hellberg through work, which undermines T3's trust-transfer mechanism.
Evidence that activity-specific segments such as hunting are not already well served by competitors.
